messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 75
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Asian
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Potter
- Trauma Type: Refugee
- Pcl5: 50

He sits on the edge of the leather chair, hands resting palms-down on his knees, fingers still dusted with pale kaolin. At seventy-five, Arjun moves with careful economy, as if the air itself might be fragile. We have met three times now, each session a slow unspooling of threads he has carried for decades. He speaks of his studio, of the wheel and the weight of wet earth, but his voice remains measured. When he describes the scent of damp clay, his shoulders tense. He tells me he works until his knuckles ache, preferring the predictable resistance of spinning stone to the silence of the house. He needs the noise, he says. The wheel must hum. His story begins in a village in South Asia that no longer exists on any map he consults. In the late seventies, the sky darkened with the march of boots and the crack of radio static. He was twenty-two, packing a canvas bag with his mother’s silver and a handful of rice, when the first mortar struck their courtyard. The memory surfaces not as a narrative, but as a physical imprint: the thick taste of ash, the violent vibration of ground through bare feet, the way his younger sister’s hand slipped from his grasp in the desperate crush of the border. He does not weep recounting this. He describes long walks on swollen legs, rationed water, cold nights pressed against strangers in a windowless warehouse, his body rigid, eyes fixed on any exit. Sleep is impossible. Every siren, every slammed gate, every raised voice pulls him back to that same stretch of asphalt. Years later, he found safety across an ocean, marrying Priya, who met him at a community center where he taught children to mold simple bowls. She knows his waking rhythms: the double-checked locks, the sharp flinch at car backfires, the way he always sits with his back to the wall in restaurants. He loves her fiercely, though he struggles to name it out loud. Some nights, he wakes to the phantom weight of a heavy blanket, his heart hammering against his ribs like a trapped bird. He breathes through it, focusing on the calluses on his own hands. They have built a quiet life in a sunlit neighborhood, but the past does not respect fences. Thunderstorms send him to the basement. The smell of burning wood in autumn makes him hold his breath until his lungs burn. He apologizes for the interruption, then returns to his tea, though the cup trembles slightly in his grip. In his studio, the pottery wheel is his anchor. When the clay yields, his hands remember how to shape, how to hold without gripping. But when a bowl collapses mid-spin, his jaw tightens, his breath shallows, and for a moment, he is not in his studio at all. He sets the piece aside, watching the street with an intensity that unsettles Priya. He speaks of the guilt that lingers like humidity—why he crossed, why his sister did not, why he still earns a living while others’ stories ended in silence. He aligns finished plates on a shelf, spacing each one exactly. Perfection feels like control. Control, he adds quietly, is the only thing he has ever been allowed to keep. He runs his thumb over a dried rim, feeling the ridge of a mistake that has been there since he was a boy. He leaves the final session with the same careful posture, pale dust on his fingertips. Outside, a siren wails. His shoulders rise toward his ears before he forces them down. He nods, says he will return next week, and steps into the afternoon light. His hands remain steady on the leather of his bag. The house is quiet. The clay waits.
